div.head: Method Explanation Evaluating touch and smell Observations
div.p: Researchers immerse themselves in a community, engaging in multisensory participation to understand the sensory experience through everyday activities like eating and walking (Howes & Classen, 1991;Pink, 2015).

Engaging with participants in sensory walkabouts or everyday activities, where they narrate and discuss their sensory experiences, allowing the ethnographer to explore these senses in real-life contexts (Low, 2015). Mostly done for smell, but touch not so much yet.

div.head: Interviews
div.p: Researchers incorporate participants' sensory experiences by conducting interviews in meaningful environments and using sensory prompts, such as sounds, images, or objects, to evoke deeper insights into their lived experiences (Harper, 2002;Pink, 2013).

For touch, the prompts can be used as well as in situ interviews where participants are asked to interact with the environment (Paterson, 2009). For smell in situ interviews can be used (Harris & Guillemin, 2011).

div.head: Sensory Diaries
div.p: This is a self-report ethnographic method where participants regularly document their sensory experiences in real-time, offering insights into the nuances of daily life and personal sensory perceptions in natural contexts (Bolger et al., 2003;Reid et al., 2011). Either in 'free of direct instruction' style, or via a questionnaire (Reid et al., 2011).

Researchers can direct participants to regularly document their smell or touch experiences in situ or from memory, such as the intensity of aromas or tactile sensations, along with emotional responses in real-life contexts et al., 2012; Rodrigues et al., 2021).

div.head: Participant-ledphotography
div.p: Participants are asked to take photographs to document their experiences and environments, often followed by interviews to

Participants can be directed in taking photographs from touch experiences, smells are more difficult to capture as they are not explore the meanings and emotions behind the images, providing deeper insights into their lives (Burles & Thomas, 2014;Warren, 2002).
visible (Pink, 2011). Yet, a photograph from the expected source could already invoke memories in the interview (Latham, 2003).

div.head: Sensory mapping
div.p: Participants are asked to document their sensory experiences, such as smells, sounds, and tactile sensations, on a map, visually representing how sensory stimuli shape perceptions of and attachments to specific places (McLean, 2020b;Misharina et al., 2023).

Participants record the locations and characteristics of tactile or olfactory experiences in an environment, with smell being commonly explored through smellwalks (McLean, 2020b) and touch requiring more guidance to capture intentional tactile interactions (Misharina et al., 2023).

div.head: Observations (through participation)
div.p: In classic participant observation in sensory ethnography, as discussed by Howes and Classen (1991), the researcher goes along with the participants while asking questions. They for example work along the employees of a to be researched companies for a certain amount of time, mostly aiming to understand the cultural and social systems of the researched group and try to see the surroundings.

However, they often overlook the experiential aspects of ethnography, focusing predominantly on visual observation (Pink, 2015). To negate this, Pink (2015) proposes a more phenomenological approach to participation in sensory ethnography, which emphasizes understanding experiences as multisensory, not just visually dominant. This method involves actively engaging through the ethnographer's own sensory experiences, beyond mere observation and interviews, to embody and share the sensory worlds of others (Pink, 2015). Ethnographers are encouraged to become emplaced within the communities they study, co-participating in the creation of place and understanding, thereby gaining deeper insights through multisensory immersion and interaction. She suggests that the ethnographer can learn through participation, particularly by focusing their engagement in the more commonplace and everyday activities such as eating and walking together with the participant, and sharing the experiences (Pink, 2015).

div.head: How does it relate to measuring the sensory modalities: smell and touch?
div.p: In the western ethnographic observations concerning sensory modalities, the focus has been very vision dominant (Howes et al., 1991;Howes & Classen, 1991;Pink, 2015;Sparkes, 2009). Yet, the other sensory modalities are not completely ignored, and observational methods have been used to study them to a certain extent. For smelling, often in an urban setting, this is often done in a walkabout (Adams et al., 2008;Low, 2015;Sparkes, 2009). These sensory walkabouts involve asking participants to narrate their sensory experiences while walking urban environments or specific areas (Low, 2015). This method provides a vivid exploration of sensory encounters within everyday spaces, shedding light on the multifaceted nature of sensory experiences in different contexts (Pink, 2015). For example Low (2015) describes having performed smell walkabouts through the city of Singapore to investigate the smellscape (olfactory environment). He walked together with the participants, experiencing and discussing the smells in the context. He argued that this approach allowed us to transition from discussing imagined smells in narrative interviews to experiencing actual in situ smells that respondents identified within specific contexts (Low, 2015). For the auditory and visual senses this can be aided by recording technology, but for smell this is more difficult, as smell is not 'recordable'. Similar methodologies are used for the observational ethnographic research on smells, often in urban settings.

Although it is not researched as often, similar methodologies could be used examining touch. It might not need to be a walk per se, but as Pink (2015) noted, an everyday, common experience where the ethnographer experiences the haptic senses together with the participant in situ.

div.head: Is it used within the workplace to measure design aspects?
div.p: Sensory observation through participation is akin to the methodology of autoethnography (Pink, 2015).

Autoethnography is a methodology that allows the ethnographer to use their own experiences to produce academic knowledge. This methodology is often used in workplace research (Orel, 2023). Although there are more layers and methods to autoethnography, observation and analysing their own experience is one of them (Orel, 2023). McGibbon et al. (2010), for example, used it in a hospital workplace setting, not as much on the sensory aspects, but more institutional. The method was combined with other methods such as alongside interviews and focus groups, to measure the stress amongst nurses (McGibbon et al., 2010). As was described above, the smellscape observations are often performed in the form of walks, often on an urban scale (Low, 2015). But this does not have to be limited to this urban scale. One could imagine a walk throughout the office building as well, or more in the traditional sense where participant and ethnographer work alongside each other for a certain amount of time, where smell of haptic experiences can be asked about at multiple instances when interacting (Howes & Classen, 1991;Pink, 2015). This is not yet a common method but does have the potential to be used more.

div.head: Is it used to measure psycho-physiological stress?
div.p: The method is inherently based on self-report and qualitative measures. Therefore, most of the observations are based on psychological stress. Observations can be made using the method of observation through participation, as Pink has described in her book (Pink, 2015). There are very few sensory ethnographic practices that specifically measure stress, but there are other ethnographic observations that do measure stress. This is for example done by McGibbon (2010). Although this is not sensory ethnography, they did aim to measure stress in the workplace amongst nurses, also using interviews and text analysis. They engaged in the daily activities and observed their everyday and every night work. During these observations, as well as during the interviews, they listened to the stories of the nurses. Questions they tried to pay attention to and answer were for example: 'What words did the nurses use to describe their experiences? How did models of nurses' stress tend to silence these standpoints? ' (McGibbon et al., 2010). This is not sensory, but it might be possible to link it to sensory aspects as well. These kind of questions could be altered towards the sensory experience, for instance on a smell walk.

There are also non-verbal indicators of behaviour amongst participants that might show stress, that could be noted during observations. These can provide valuable insights when certain emotions are not recognised and/or verbalized. Mohiyeddini and Semple (2013) identified displacement behaviours linked to stress, such as grooming, hand-face contact, yawning, fumbling, and lip-biting. Fidgeting, including object manipulation (e.g., pens), is also a common stress response (Woodward & Kanjo, 2021). Their fidget cube, using deep learning classifiers, offers an objective tool to assess and mitigate stress. Dael et al. (2012a, 2012b) developed the Body Action and Posture Coding System (BAP) to link body movements to emotions, while Koldijk et al. (2018) created an automatic classifier to infer workplace stress from multimodal sensor data. Their study found posture most effective in distinguishing stress levels, with facial expressions enhancing accuracy. Though these observations are not strictly sensory ethnographic, they could complement such methods with additional and maybe more objective insights.

div.head: Interviews
div.p: Sensory ethnography, as discussed by Pink (2015), expands traditional interviews by integrating sensory experiences, providing deeper insights into participants' lived experiences (Calvey, 2021).

Instead of relying solely on verbal communication, this approach encourages active engagement with sensory environments. One method is conducting interviews in meaningful or research-relevant settings, allowing both interviewer and participant to remain active in the environment. This helps capture how sensory contexts influence experiences. Rather than being seated and stationary, interviews can take place while moving through a space, fostering a more natural and immersive discussion (Pink, 2015). Another approach is mediated interviews, where sensory prompts-such as images, sounds, textures, or personally significant objects-help participants recall and articulate experiences in greater detail (Harper, 2002;Pink, 2013). This method transforms interviews into reflective and interactive processes, enhancing memory recall and encouraging richer descriptions of sensory perceptions.

Interviews are often used alongside other ethnographic methods such as observations (McGibbon et al., 2010) and participant-led photography, which will be elaborated on in a later chapter (Harper, 2002;Latham, 2003;Pilcher et al., 2016). Conducting interviews in meaningful settings and using sensory elicitation can enhance understanding of participants' sensory subjectivity and contextual meanings (Pink, 2015). Since knowledge, practices, and experiences are shaped by personal and cultural factorsand individuals shift between subjectivities-researchers must critically reflect on their role in knowledge production. Harris and Guillemin (2014) demonstrated the benefits of sensory ethnography in healthcare research by asking participants to describe sensory elements like smells and sounds, uncovering aspects of experience often overlooked in traditional interviews. By capturing a full range of sensory information, these methods provide rich, immersive data that reveal how individuals perceive and interact with their surroundings. They also make interviews more engaging and meaningful for participants, as they reflect comprehensively on their lived experiences (Guillemin & Harris, 2014;Pink, 2015). However, sensory interviews can be complex and time-consuming, and the subjectivity of sensory experiences makes data analysis challenging, particularly when participants freely define sensory prompts (Calvey, 2021).

div.head: How does it relate to the sensory modalities: smell and touch?
div.p: Smell has been proven to have a strong effect in recollection of memories, which would make smell elicitation a useful method to help recall memories (Harris & Guillemin, 2011). Although interview questions such as 'What did that place smell like?' or 'Is there a smell that particularly reminds you of that time?' (Guillemin & Harris, 2014) can be asked, elicitation might be a little bit more difficult. Smells are difficult to capture, bring with, visualise or control, especially when researching the smells of a certain area (compared to a perfume) (Pink, 2015). There are examples of scratch-n-sniff studies where participants were asked to answer questions on experience and induced memories, which could be translated into an interview setting (Guillemin & Harris, 2014;McLean, 2020b). Yet, this is a rather complex method to execute. The most effective way might be to place the interviews in the studied environment, more in a observational/participatory way (Pink, 2015). This way, the smells are very present and can help elicit the memories. Unfortunately, this still comes with the sidenote that the smells are still difficult to control. An area might smell differently on different days or even different times of the day.

Touch too is a very important sense in the recollection of memories, which can be used in interviews as well as by using the materiality of an object, as through a line of questions and elicitation that tap into the tactile sensations such as movement and texture (Paterson, 2009). These elicitations can be in the form of objects as well as photographs of the objects and environments that is in the research objective. Even though, the use of photographs or other visual elicitation as drawings is inherently a visual task, the photographs are not just visual images, but contain other sensory information as well (Guillemin & Harris, 2014;Pink, 2015). For example the materiality of objects in the photograph, participants might remember or imagine what it might feel like, through embodied touch (Mallgrave, 2018). These prompts do not necessarily need to be preselected by the researcher but could also be indicated during the interview encounter, initiated by either the interviewer but also by the interviewee (Harris & Guillemin, 2011). Deriving from this, it would be important that the location of the interview would be set in the to be studied context and environment.

div.head: Is it used in the workplace to measure design
div.p: Interviews are widely used in office design research but often follow a traditional, stationary, talkcentred format (Pink, 2015). Pink argues this limits understanding, as sensory experiences are also expressed through gestures, facial expressions, and touch. Interviews are also used in the new trend of participatory design, often combining interviews with workshops (Markkanen et al., 2022), but the interviews remain largely verbal. Similarly, workplace focus groups note body language and tone but often overlook elicitation methods or environmental context, potentially losing valuable insights (Golvani et al., 2021). Pink (2015) emphasizes that interviews should take place in meaningful settings, such as participants' desks or while walking through the office, to reveal sensory insights like seating comfort or airflow.

When on-site interviews are not possible, elicitation methods-such as object or photo prompts-can enhance engagement. Warren (2008) used photo-elicitation in design aesthetics research, incorporating participant-led photography to capture emotions and storytelling, recognizing that aesthetics are difficult to express through language. She also emphasized understanding participants' cultural backgrounds, aligning with Pink's (2015) view on the importance of first researching the (inter-)subjectivity of both the researcher and the participant. So although interviews are often used in workplace design, only few instances this is done in a rich ethnographic way as described by Pink and Warren.
Is it used to measure psycho-physiological stress?

Interviews, though not widely used as a primary method for studying stress in workplace design, have proven to be valuable in exploring stress-related experiences. According to Bergefurt et al.(2021), only a small percentage of research on stress in workplace design utilizes interviews. However, interviews, particularly focus groups, have yielded important insights. For instance, Golvani et al. (2021) examined the experiences of nurses working in no-daylight environments through focus group interviews.

Although stress was not the primary focus of their study, open-ended questions like "What is your experience regarding limited access to daylight during a workday?" revealed that heightened stress was frequently mentioned by participants, which was uncovered in the thematic analysis, and described in those themes as result.

In contrast, a study by McGibbon et al. (2010) directly focused on stress, combined interviews with other ethnographic methods such as observations and focus groups. Their in-depth interview questions, such as "Tell me about some of the challenges in your work?" and "How do you manage these challenges?" provided insights into the personal and professional factors contributing to stress (McGibbon et al., 2010). The researchers went beyond the literal answers, examining the language nurses used to describe their experiences and considering how dominant models of stress might suppress alternative viewpoints (McGibbon et al., 2010). This approach aligns with Pink's (2015) view that interviews should focus not only on spoken words but also on the nuances of expression and context.
By incorporating participant observation, McGibbon et al. gained deeper insights into stress in the nursing profession (McGibbon et al., 2010).

div.head: Sensory diary
div.p: A diary is a sequential documentation of participants' activities and experiences, capturing ongoing social, psychological, and physiological processes in everyday contexts (Bolger et al., 2003). As selfreport tools, diaries provide valuable insights into daily life by recording small yet significant experiences (Bolger et al., 2003). They are widely used across psychology, healthcare, product development, and food research (Chen et al., 2012;Jacelon & Imperio, 2005;Reid et al., 2011;Rodrigues et al., 2021). These diaries are often question-prompted, and Bolger and colleagues (2003) emphasize the importance of aligning the research question with the research design.

Diary studies typically follow three protocols: interval-contingent (regular reporting at fixed intervals), signal-contingent (entries prompted by random or fixed signals), and event-contingent (entries triggered by specific events) (Bolger et al., 2003). Diaries can also be easily used alongside other methods such as diary-interviews and diary-photography (Latham, 2003). In diary-interviews, participants first document their daily experiences, thoughts, and feelings, which are later explored in-depth during an interview. Adding disposable cameras allows participants to visually capture meaningful moments, further enriching discussions (Latham, 2003). The role of participant-led photography will be elaborated in the next chapter.

A key advantage of diaries is their ability to capture experiences in real time, reducing retrospective bias and providing richer contextual data compared to traditional methods (Reid et al., 2011). Reflexive diary writing can also serve as a tool for self-reflection and behavioural change, making it particularly useful for sensory ethnography. However, diaries rely on self-reporting, which can introduce biases such as social desirability or incomplete entries due to participant discretion (Reid et al., 2011).
Maintaining long-term engagement can also be challenging, though digital diary tools offering short, automated prompts help mitigate this issue (Bolger et al., 2003;Reid et al., 2011).

div.head: How does it relate to the sensory modalities: smell and touch?
div.p: When studying sensory experiences through diaries, researchers often focus on smell and touch alongside other senses. Participants typically document their overall sensory perceptions with specific prompts. Rodrigues et al. (2021) examined cheese consumption, asking participants to record contextual details along with sensory perceptions and emotions. While 23 sensory characteristics were noted, only two-'strong aroma' and 'mild aroma'-related to smell. Touch-related attributes, primarily concerning mouthfeel, included 'greasiness,' 'soft,' 'harder,' and 'thicker crust,' underscoring its significance in cheese perception. Chen et al. (2012) explored sensory importance in early product experiences using diaries and interviews. Over four weeks of home use, participants tracked sensory aspects of an orange juicer. Touch was most critical, first for exploration and later for evaluating fatigue, comfort, and pain, which heightened stress. Smell, though less emphasized, evoked positive emotions through the scent of fresh juice.

These studies highlight how diaries can capture multisensory experiences. It does seem of importance to specifically ask to describe each sensory modality (or the ones that are to be researched) separately and distinctively. This is due to our highly visually dominant mindset (Pink, 2015), if questions are too open, less dominant or focussed modalities such as smell and touch might not be reported on as much or as profoundly.

div.head: Is it used in the workplace to measure design
div.p: The diary method is mentioned as a frequently used method to study the experiences close to the time of their occurrence, as well as in real-life setting which cannot be studied in laboratory form (Soucek et al., 2023). Generally in the workplace, it is not always scaled under ethnographic method but also as predominantly quantitative self-report questionnaires (Soucek et al., 2023). This quantitative aspects makes it less ethnographic, but as they mention, there are different types of diary study designs. Soucek (2023) mentions two examples where the diary method was applied in office design (Lindberg et al., 2018;Soucek et al., 2023;Thayer et al., 2010), both mostly focused on visual and acoustic aspects of the office environment, and their relation to employee stress. They both compared participant experiences over multiple consecutive days, in the different environments: private office, high partition cubicle or open bench (Lindberg et al., 2018) and no skylight, no window view vs skylight and window view (Thayer et al., 2010). Beattie and Griffin (2014) too mentioned using the diary method by means of using surveys for over the course of 8 days. To research the effect of experiences of incivility at work on two outcomes, stress and engagement, at a within-person level they used 4 validated questionnaires using Likert scales. So here too, the diary is interpreted as qualitative self-report measurement using questionnaires, opposed to more open ended, qualitative questions. Although, this method does make for a more objective analysis and lower participant burden, it does negate the previously mentioned advantages of a natural, spontaneous and deeper level responses and reflection. Poppleton et al. (2008) do have an example of using qualitative questions in their research in work-life balance among companies, instead of workplace design. Here the diary consists of a short summary of the events and activities of the day, and then a longer section consisting of elaboration questions related to the topic (Poppleton et al., 2008). So there are examples of qualitative use of the diary method, yet it seems to be less frequently used, and often not concerning workplace design.
Is it used to measure psycho-physiological stress?

As mentioned above, the chapter of Soucek et al. (2023) mentioned two examples of office design being compared to psycho-physiological stress using the diary method. In one example they explored the association of workplace design and employee health and wellbeing, with physiological stress as heartrate variability and perceived stress levels via smartphone app (Soucek et al., 2023). Another example mentioned, investigated how physical workspace features affect employee stress by room size and windows. Using cardiac monitoring, cortisol sampling, and hourly self-reports, they assessed physiological and psychological stress responses alongside environmental satisfaction (Soucek et al., 2023). These are all quantitative stress measurement (psychological and physiological) methods that are less ethnographic but are well-researched and validated. But there are also diary methods measuring stress that are more qualitative. Clarkson and Hodgkinson (1999) the quantitative application focus, and aimed to explore e more 'free response format', qualitative style to complement this quantitative measurement. In this free format, participants were presented with a diary booklet in which they were requested to record self-identified critical incidents that had triggered a perception of stress, their feelings and their perceived consequences. The format was free but the daily explanation did include prompt questions as: 'What was the source of the stress', 'What was the consequence of that stress (how did it make you think, feel behave. Did this have effect on you personally/the organisation?)' and 'How did you cope' (Clarkson & Hodgkinson, 1999). They found this method to be a useful method to complement traditional questionnaires to gain deeper insights in the experiences of occupational stress (Clarkson & Hodgkinson, 1999). Mazzola et al. (2011) also stress the importance of qualitative methods in addition to quantitative measures, especially in work-related stress research, as there can be any variety of stressors, the provision of context and gaining deeper understanding is key. They too discuss examples of more qualitative ways of performing diary research, but in a bit less free format. They describe the method to include open ended survey questions which are answered at certain times of the day, where the participant experiences a stressful event. There seems to be a range on how free the diary method can be applied to measure psychological stress, each with its own pro's and con's, where at least the addition of gaining qualitative data has been identified as very valuable.

div.head: Participant-led-photography
div.p: Participant-led photography, also known as visual diaries or photo-voice, is a qualitative research method where participants take photographs to document their experiences, surroundings, and daily lives (Burles & Thomas, 2014;Pilcher et al., 2016). Rooted in participatory research, this method allows participants to actively contribute to data collection, enhancing its authenticity (Pilcher et al., 2016).
Typically, participants receive instructions related to the research topic and take photos accordingly.

These images are then used in interviews or focus groups to facilitate discussions and elicit deeper insights into participants' memories, emotions, and meanings attached to the photos (Burles & Thomas, 2014;Latham, 2003). This combination of photography and interviews helps capture narratives closer to the actual experiences, improving accuracy (Latham, 2003). While most studies use participant-led photography alongside interviews, some quantitative approaches exist, such as analysing uploaded images with digital tools (Bakolis et al., 2018). Another emerging method involves using Instagram for research, either as a digital life archive or a platform for storytelling and data sharing (Shortt & Warren, 2020).

The main advantage of this method is its ability to capture habitual aspects of daily life that might go unnoticed in traditional research (Pilcher et al., 2016). It enables participants to reflect on and articulate experiences beyond verbal communication, making research more engaging and insightful (Burles & Thomas, 2014). However, limitations exist-visual diaries may reflect a selective self-representation rather than a full depiction of daily life. Additionally, translating abstract or emotional experiences into photographs can be challenging, particularly when dealing with sensitive topics (Burles & Thomas, 2014). Moreover, not all aspects of daily life are visible or easily photographed, limiting the method's ability to capture intangible experiences (Burles & Thomas, 2014).

div.head: How does it relate to the sensory modalities: smell and touch?
div.p: Photography is inherently a visual concept, and is therefore mostly linked to visual research. Yet, this

does not mean that it cannot play a valuable role in the research of other sensory modalities. The sense of smell, or olfaction, is notoriously difficult to document and study because it lacks a direct visual component. However, participant-led photography could still play a role in capturing the contexts and sources of olfactory experiences. Participants can photograph places, objects, and activities associated with particular smells, thereby providing visual proxies for olfactory data (Pink, 2011). For instance, a participant might document the kitchen where they prepare food, a garden with fragrant flowers, or a marketplace with diverse aromas. These images could help recover memories (Latham, 2003), and combined with participants' narratives about the smells they experience, could offer valuable insights into the cultural and personal significance of olfaction.

By incorporating the sense of touch, researchers can explore how tactile experiences, along with other sensory modalities, are intertwined with visual ones (Pink, 2011). Pictures taken during the research can depict materiality, patterns and textures of the participants surrounding (Shortt & Warren, 2020).

For example, participants might photograph their hands touching different materials, capturing the sensory qualities of these interactions through embodied touch. These images can then be analysed to understand the role of touch in participants' daily lives and how it contributes to their overall sensory experience. This method aligns with Pink's argument that visual and sensory ethnography must account for the multisensory nature of environments and experiences, recognizing that images can evoke and represent non-visual senses through associative and contextual means (Pink, 2011).Although, these arguments show that there could be potential to use participant-led photography, in combination with interviews and/or diaries, as a method to research touch and smell, there seem to be little to no cases where this has explicitly been done.

div.head: Is it used in the workplace to measure design
div.p: The use of participant-led photography in workplace design research remains rather limited, but not entirely uncommon. Warren has explored its application in several studies (Shortt & Warren, 2019, 2020;Warren, 2002Warren, , 2008)). She found that words alone were insufficient to describe workplace environments, leading her to ask participants to take Pictures with the briefing: 'Show me what it feels like to work here', which were then discussed and contextualised in interviews (Warren, 2002). She argued not to over-emphasize the importance of the visual as these images often conveyed underlying emotions or rituals. For examples a photograph of cookie bags symbolizing a sense of community. This notion under scribes the importance of interviews and notes alongside the photography. A later study used the same method to evaluate a redesigned office space, reinforcing the value of combining photography with interviews (Warren, 2008). This combination of participant-led photography in combination with interviews was also performed by Pataki-Bitto (2024), where she asked employees with a hybrid work schedule to photograph office elements that inspired their work or boosted wellbeing, followed by interviews to discuss the meaning behind their photos. Through this qualitative method she was able to uncover that the social, cultural and shared memory influences in the workplace environment to have a big influence on the employee perceived wellbeing (Pataki-Bitto, 2024). The sensory aspects was not focused on.

Despite critiques regarding analysis, Shortt and Warren introduced Grounded Visual Pattern Analysis (GVPA) to systematically interpret visual data, integrating dialogical and archaeological analysis (Shortt & Warren, 2019). They demonstrated its use in an ethnographic study of hair salon workers, uncovering insights into workplace environments and identity formation. Herneoja et al. (2023) also applied a less photography method that was then analysed by systematic models. They analysed the participants gaze and view from their workstation, and asked participants to take pictures through a smartphone application, attaching location and time stamps (Herneoja et al., 2023). These more systematically and technically analysed methods might help in removing subjectivity and help recognising patterns, but it lacks in the ability for participants to attach meaning and context to the pictures and design elements, which is essentially the key benefit of ethnography. Although research on participant-led photography in office design remains fairly limited, there is some work that highlights its potential beyond visual aspects, emphasizing its effectiveness when combined with interviews.

div.head: Is it used to measure psycho-physiological stress?
div.p: Participant-led photography is often used to explore general experiences rather than focusing on a single concept like stress (Burles & Thomas, 2014;Latham, 2003;Pilcher et al., 2016;Warren, 2002). While stress may emerge as a theme, most studies use open-ended prompts, allowing for a broader, more holistic perspective (Glaw et al., 2017). However, this approach can make specific measurements more challenging.

Some studies have applied participant-led photography to examine distress more directly. For example, Kantrowitz-Gordon and Vandermause (2016) investigated distress among new parents of premature babies by asking them to take digital photos over 2-4 weeks that represented their feelings after bringing their baby home. These images were later discussed in interviews, helping parents articulate their experiences and making distress more tangible through metaphor (Kantrowitz-Gordon & Vandermause, 2016). Other research has combined participant-led photography with quantitative psychological stress measures. Jiang et al. (2019) studied sweatshop workers' perceptions of outdoor environments by asking them to photograph spaces that influenced their mental state. Participants then selected three key photos, reflected on them for a minute, and completed a stress and anxiety questionnaire before discussing their emotions and memories (Jiang et al., 2019). Similarly, Girang et al. (2022) used participant-led photography and walk-along interviews to explore stress-alleviating spaces on a university campus.

Their focus was on social settings, distinguishing between high-and low-energy environments and solitude versus social interaction. By combining photography, mapping, and interviews, they identified which environments were sought out in different emotional and stress-related situations (Girang et al., 2022).

These studies demonstrate that participant-led photography can be valuable for investigating stress, particularly when combined with interviews or quantitative measures. However, its strength lies in capturing the complexity of experiences rather than isolating single variables.

div.head: Sensory mapping
div.p: Sensory mapping depicts the world as it is subjectively experienced through various human senses, combining aesthetics with empirical data to highlight personal, time-specific realities and the morethan-visual characteristics of places. Contemporary practitioners use diverse sensory media to emphasize the emotional, embodied, and affective dimensions of cartography (McLean, 2020b). Most of the sensory maps used, are single-sense maps, focussing on one of the five main senses yet there are also attempts of performing the method multi-sensory (Misharina et al., 2023). The representation of the sense, however, does not always have to be in the medium of original encounter (McLean, 2020b).

The medium of the map is often visual even though the researched sense might not be. Sensory mapping often explores how sensory stimuli influence human perception and experience of space. It investigates the qualitative aspects of sensory experiences and how these contribute to the understanding and attachment to specific places (Misharina et al., 2023).

Sensory mapping is typically performed by providing participants with a base map of the area to be studied, which they use to record their sensory experiences (Misharina et al., 2023). Participants are encouraged to note down impressions such as specific smells, sounds, and tactile sensations at various locations. These impressions are often marked using color-coded stickers on the map, which represent different types of sensory stimuli (Misharina et al., 2023). The mapping process quite often include wandering through the area, allowing sensory stimuli to guide the participants' paths and experiences (McLean, 2020b), very comparable to the sensory walks mentioned in in the section of observations (Pink, 2015). Data collected from individual maps are then digitized and analysed collectively to identify patterns and create a comprehensive sensory map of the area (Misharina et al., 2023). An example of method was proposed by Degen et al. (2016) from a workshop they gave, using sensory mapping through a Neighbourhood in London as example. They proposed creating three maps. The first map captures sensory experiences: smells, sights, textures, and sounds. The second map records subjective experiences from interviews, detailing feelings about the space as hostile, friendly, oppressive, etc. The third map, a 'relationship map,' asks users why they perceive the space in those ways. The goal is to merge the researcher's observations with the users' experiences to create 'places of translation' (Degen et al., 2016). It is important to question what the added advantage of the mapping would be to the sensory walks in itself. It does create a more visual output, but it might also aid in the reflection and recollection process of the sensory experiences, rather similarly as participant-ledphotography does.

div.head: How does it relate to the sensory modalities: smell and touch?
div.p: Sensory mapping is a multisensory methodology that explores all five senses, with smell being the most commonly studied, followed by sound and vision (McLean, 2020b). Smell maps are often created through smell walks, where participants navigate an environment, identifying and documenting smells.

Sometimes, they are blindfolded to enhance perception. The recorded data-locations, sources, and characteristics of smells-are then visualized in various formats, including Scratch-n-sniff walls, 3D tactile maps, and traditional 2D visual maps (McLean, 2020b). Smell mapping helps localize odours, understand their environmental interactions (e.g., wind, humidity), and document their cultural significance. McLean's (2012) city smell maps (e.g., Edinburgh, Amsterdam) use modified cartographic symbols to depict scent dispersion, while others use dots to highlight humidity-driven scent landscapes.

Touch, however, is rarely studied in sensory mapping. Misharina et al. (2023) found that participants often overlooked touch in a city-based multisensory study. They found that people perceived two categories of touch: 1) being touched by an object, human or weather, and 2) the experience of intentionally reaching to touch something. The last category, the conscious choice, often came with the revelation that the experienced tactile properties often did not match the visually perceived and expected tactile properties (Misharina et al., 2023). From this example we can learn that researching touch in a mapping method is certainly possible, but it is important to guide the participants well in including touch in their conscious experience. This suggests that studying touch through mapping requires prompting participants to be more consciously aware of their tactile experiences. Touch is more commonly integrated as an output in tactile mapping rather than as an input for analysis (McLean, 2020b).

div.head: Is it used in the workplace to measure design
div.p: Sensory mapping is often performed in an urban scale involving a city or neighbourhood setting (Degen et al., 2016;McLean, 2020b;Misharina et al., 2023), letting participants walk through a neighbourhood, and map out their experiences on a map. One might consider whether a similar method could be applied in an office environment using an office layout map. Given the smaller scale and distances, the predominantly indoor environment, and the likely uniform design theme throughout the building, the observed differences may be less pronounced than in an urban setting. However, this does not diminish the method's potential usefulness. Variations likely exist within the office layout, with certain areas being more popular for specific activities and providing distinct sensory inputs. These differences could still be effectively mapped on an office layout plan. There is an example of an indoor setting where a smellscape sensory map has been performed in a hospital corridor (McLean, 2020a). This project investigated how hospitals can be understood through their unique smellscape, formed by interactions of people, cleaning equipment, and food (McLean, 2020a). A virtual map, requiring imaginative engagement, captures smells from weak coffee near the canteen to metallic blood in operating theatres.

Research involved gathering simplified smell descriptions from open-ended questions posed to friends and colleagues, with artistic interpretations of these smells presented as "smell shapes." The smells were colour coded an visualised creatively on a map of the corridors (see figure 1, (McLean, 2020a)). These indoor settings are very rare for sensory mapping, but this example does show that it is certainly possible and possibly quite helpful. Although, this is not an office setting, but it is a workplace. The application of the method would not be too different.

div.head: Is it used to measure psycho-physiological stress?
div.p: Sensory mapping is rarely used to measure stress specifically. Measurements that come closest are measures of emotion. For example Hogertz (2010) measured the arousal dimensions of emotions of high-low arousal against positive-negative, where stress is in the negative arousing quadrant (Hogertz, 2010). They used real-time electrodermal activity (EDA) as an indicator of emotional brain processing, which was then compared with arousal-eliciting environments on the path the participant walked and projected on an emotional arousal map. This is an example of physiological measurement, but most mapping research is done with psychological measurements, where people comment on their emotions during the walking a qualitative form (Mclean, 2012;McLean, 2020a;Misharina et al., 2023). For example in a study using a scratch and sniff map, participants were asked to freely add sticky notes with places or feelings the smell reminded them of (Mclean, 2012). This way it is difficult to capture stress, or any specific emotion, but more useful for a more explorative method.
Rationale for the empirical study

Now that the literature has shed some light on the existing body of research, both on sensory effects on psycho-physiological stress in the workplace environment, as on sensory ethnographic techniques, the next step is to answer the sub-question: What can we learn about the relationship between sensory ethnographic techniques found in the literature review and psycho-physiological stress resulting from the physical workplace environment? To answer this question a pilot study was conducted.

From the literature was found that there was a body of work of visual and auditory influences of the workplace environment on stress, yet the sensory dimensions of smell and touch were largely neglected.

This pilot study will therefor focus on these two modalities. From the literature we also found that traditional quantitative measurements often lack depth and context insights to evaluate the sensory experiences and effects (Gobo, 2011;McGibbon et al., 2010;Pink, 2013), whereas sensory ethnography is sensitive to being very subjective (Pink, 2015). This pilot study will therefore combine more traditional quantitative methodologies for measuring psychological as well as physiological stress with sensory ethnographic measurements to answer the sub question: What can we learn about the relationship between sensory ethnographic techniques found in the literature review and psychophysiological stress resulting from the physical workplace environment?

To do so, this pilot set up an experiment where we expose participants to 4 different environments. In these rooms the sensory modalities of touch and smell will be manipulated, as the literature study found that those senses have been under researched, but could provide interesting results (Pallasmaa, 1994;Spence, 2020a). Their experiences will be evaluated both by sensory ethnographic techniques of focus groups and sensory diaries. The focus groups were chosen as from literature was found that many sensory ethnographic techniques are combined with focus groups or interviews, as they seem to provide much context and understanding in underlying mechanisms and reasoning (Bolger et al., 2003;Latham, 2003;Low, 2015;McLean, 2020a;Pink, 2015). The diary studies were described as an effective means to gain in situ information (Bolger et al., 2003;Latham, 2003), especially ass the focus-groups are not possible to be held in situ.

By exposing participants to different environments within a single day, the study aimed to simulate the variety of sensory experiences that might be encountered over a week, while keeping the data collection manageable. This approach also allowed for a comparison of the subjective experience of the environments and psychological stress, and the physiological stress responses to understand how both sensory input and personal perception affect stress levels.

div.head: Study design
div.p: This experiment employed a 2 (materiality: hard vs. soft) x 2 (scent (odourless vs. citrus) within-subject design. Participants worked in four environments over the course of a single workday. Participants' responses were measured using a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods across three types of data collection: objective physiological stress measurement (EDA, HRV), self-reported stress (EMA), Sensory Diary, and Focus groups.

div.head: Participants
div.p: Participants were a convenience sample from the students and employee population of Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e) invited via the JF Schouten participant database and direct on-campus recruitment. All participants received a compensation of 30 euros for their time and involvement in the study. A total of 20 to 30 participants were deemed necessary to ensure sufficient data collection and variability, yet due to monetary and time-restrictions, only 14 participants were recruited from which 3 dropped out due to personal and scheduling issues resulting in 11 participants. Although a mix of students and employees would have been preferred, the entire participant group was made up of TU/e students (5 women, 6 men), due to the time consuming study.
To be eligible for the study, participants had to meet the following criteria (Beil & Hanes, 2013):
• Be at least 18 years old.
• Be able to read and speak English.
• Have no heart conditions, or epilepsy.
• Not be taking medications such as antidepressants or beta-blockers (although participants taking oral contraceptives or light painkillers, such as ibuprofen, were allowed to participate).
• Not regularly experiencing panic or anxiety that might be triggered by stress.
Since the study involved reflecting on sensory experiences, individuals with conditions that could impair their ability to perceive sensory input were excluded. This included participants with:
• Impaired sense of smell (e.g., Anosmia. Also including temporary conditions, such a due to the flu or COVID-19).
• Impaired or decreased haptic (touch) perception.
• Uncorrected visual impairments, such as colour blindness.

div.head: Procedure
div.p: Participants completed the study over the course of a single day, experiencing four different preselected environments in a within-subject design. Each day a maximum of four participants was possible, the complete week schedule can be found in appendix B. Figure 3 shows the procedure, followed by a step by step explanation. T-15 At 09:00 welcome, explanation, informed consent and sensor application. Upon arrival, participants were greeted and introduced to the study giving a brief overview of the day's activities, ensuring they understood the purpose of the research and their role. After reviewing and signing the informed consent form, they were connected to physiological monitoring equipment. T-5 Acclimation period. The participants were getting settled into the room and take out their stuff. These 5 minutes of data are not used in the analysis.

T0 Work or study tasks. In each environment, participants engaged in a 50-minute work session. The tasks were partially controlled to ensure consistency across participants, with activities focused on quiet, individual work such as reading or writing. Participants were asked to avoid phone calls, meetings, moving around, eating or any other highly engaging activities during this time to prevent confounding effects on stress levels. T+50 EMA questionnaire and sensory diary. The participants were given 10-15 minutes to consider their environment and complete a sensory diary and EMA questionnaire. T+60 Washout period. between environments, participants underwent a 15-minute washout period or break to minimize any lingering effects from the previous setting. During this time, participants were asked to not engage in any heartrate altering activities such as physical activity.

The steps above were repeated for all four environments, with participants moving from one sensory condition to the next in a randomized order. Each participant was exposed to both soft and hard textures, as well as smell and no-smell environments. The work tasks remained consistent across the conditions to ensure comparability.

End-of-Day Focus Group. At the end of the day, participants took part in a focus group to discuss their overall experiences in each environment and reflect on their stress responses. Photograph probes were used to prompt discussions about the sensory aspects of each environment. Prior to the focus group, the researcher conducted a quick preliminary analysis of the sensory diaries and psychological stress data to tailor the discussion and ask more directed questions based on initial findings.

By the end of the day, each participant had experienced all four environments, allowing for a comprehensive comparison of both objective and subjective stress responses across different sensory conditions. The precise time-schedule can be found in appendix A.

div.head: Location
div.p: The study took place in the Atlas building of Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e), using two designated spaces: General Purpose Lab 1 and the Gameplay Lab. Both labs were used to simulate the four different environmental conditions by varying the furnishings while keeping the same physical room layout (See figure 4 and 5). All rooms featured large windows to provide a consistent natural light source across conditions. Each participant experienced all four environments for an hour over the course of a single day, with each environment's sensory manipulation carefully controlled.
Four distinct environments were created by combining the presence or absence of a pleasant citrussy smell with soft or hard material textures.

div.head: Smell Dimensions
div.p: In this study, participants were exposed to either a citrussy aroma or no smell. To ensure consistency, aroma oils were used to diffuse the smell throughout the room, as these oils are often rated as pleasant and can maintain a relatively stable concentration over time (Herz, 2009;Spence, 2020b). The scent was distributed by a stick-diffuser from H&M winter spices, including citrus and ginger notes as well as warm spices such as cloves, almonds and vanilla which are generally considered pleasant and are congruent with the time of year (Herz, 2009;Spence, 2020b).

div.head: Texture Dimensions
div.p: The texture manipulation involved staging rooms with either soft or hard materials to influence the tactile sensory experience. The "soft" rooms were furnished with items such as couches, poufs, blankets, pillows, tablecloths, and curtains, while the "hard" rooms were outfitted with hard tables, plastic chairs, and other rigid materials. The orientation, monitor set-up and chairs were the same in all four rooms.

To confirm the validity of these manipulations, the thesis supervisors evaluated each room after staging to ensure that the furniture and materials accurately represented "soft" or "hard" environments.

div.head: Data collection
div.p: We employed a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods across four types of data collection: objective physiological Stress measurement (EDA, HRV), self-reported stress (EMA), sensory diary, and focus groups.

div.head: Physiological Stress Measurements
div.p: To monitor physiological stress, two key biometric indicators are used: heart rate variability (HRV) and electrodermal activity (EDA) (Yin et al., 2020). Both are measured using the Mobi-8 device, recording to via the desktop app PhyLo. The HRV electrodes are placed using the 3 electrode system as per device instructions (left clavicle, right clavicle, left underneath ribcage). It collected raw data from a singlechannel electrocardiogram (ECG), which was then used to derive secondary parameters such as HRV.

The sampling rate was set at 1024 Hz. For HRV, we calculated a time-domain indicator: the root mean square of successive differences between normal heartbeats (RMSSD, in milliseconds [ms]). A higher RMSSD value reflects increased parasympathetic activity, which implies stress reduction.

EDA measures the electrical conductance of the skin, which increases with sweat gland activity driven by sympathetic nervous system arousal, measuring the galvanic skin response (GSR). It was measured via finger electrodes, placed on the fingertips of the ring and middle finger of the non-dominant hand, using Velcro wrapping, as per device instructions. Due to lacking time, and noisy data caused by usage of the hands during the deskwork, this EDA data has not been processed and used.

To minimise disturbances in the physiological data, the participants were instructed to remain seated, not eat during the measurement time, refrain from drinking caffeinated drinks that day, not excessively drink alcohol from the night before or perform (heavy) physical activity that day

div.head: Psychological Stress Measurements
div.p: Momentary affect was assessed as proxy for psychological stress, using a questionnaire measuring the three-dimension core affect model by Schimmack and Grobb (2000) including the dimensions: Pleasure-Arousal-Tension (PAT). Each dimension was represented by three bipolar indicators, calculated by subtracting opposing affective states. Participants rated 18 mood items on a 4-point scale (1 = I do not feel it, 2 = I feel it slightly, 3 = I feel it moderately , 4 = I feel it strongly), following a standardized instruction. The items for each dimension were: pleasant-unpleasant, positive negative, and good-bad for pleasure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.7); awake-sleepy, alert-tired, and wakeful-drowsy for awake (Cronbach's alpha = 0.9); and restless-at rest, tense-relaxed, jittery-calm for tension (Cronbach's alpha = 0.9) (Schimmack & Grob, 2000).

Participants completed the questionnaire in each of the rooms after the working session while seated in the study environment, using the m-Path app on their smartphones. The complete questionnaire can be found in appendix C.

div.head: Sensory Diary
div.p: A semi-structured diary method was employed to capture participants' subjective sensory experiences in each environment. This diary combined open-ended questions with Likert scale ratings, allowing for both rich qualitative and quantitative data collection (Bolger et al., 2003;Latham, 2003;Pink, 2015).

By directing participants' attention to specific sensory modalities-particularly smell and touch, which are often less consciously perceived-this method encouraged more focused reflection on the sensory aspects of each environment, while still being present in the environment for optimal recollection as they are still in the environment experiencing the senses (Pink, 2015). The diary consisted of questions organized into sections for each of the four sensory modalities: vision, sound, smell, and touch.

Additionally, general questions about the overall sensory experience, frequency, and intensity of stimuli were included. The questions about vision and auditory experiences were asked as well, to help avoid skewing participants' attention away from the primary sensory dimensions being studied (smell and touch) and still provide a holistic overview of their sensory experiences (Pink, 2015;Spence, 2020a).
The sensory appraisal questions were formulated as follows: 'How would you rate the smell in the room?' With a follow-up open ended question asking them to explain the rating.

Participants were asked to fill out the sensory diary digitally on their smartphones immediately after completing the ecological momentary assessment (EMA) questionnaire in each environment, using the same software: m-Path. Digital diaries were chosen based on recommendations from Bolger (2003), who highlighted that digital methods enhance data accuracy by allowing real-time time-stamping, reducing participant forgetfulness, increasing reflection, and minimizing errors in data entry. The complete diary questionnaire, including all questions and scales used, can be found in Appendix D.

div.head: Focus group
div.p: At the end of the study day, participants engaged in a focus group to discuss their experiences in the four different environments. The focus group was conducted on the same day to ensure that participants' memories of the environments were still fresh. The amount of participants per group was dependent on how many participants signed up for the day, ranging from one (interview) to four. During the day, the researcher performed a preliminary analysis of the diary and stress data on the first three rooms. This quick review looked at the diary and EMA results of the first three rooms. The (large) noticeable differences in EMA and quantitative sensory ratings were compared per room manually, and aligned with the open question answers. This helped form more directed and relevant questions during the focus group discussion, enriching the data collection with deeper insights.

The focus group followed a structured approach based on Hennink et al. (2020). The session unfolded in the following stages: Introduction and explanation, introductory warm-up questions, key questions (focused on smell and touch experiences, and based on diary entries), closing question and conclusion and thanking of the participants. The complete focus groups guide can be found in appendix E. The focus group ran until saturation, but generally lasted between 20 -30 minutes. The discussions were audio-recorded via MS Teams as well as using the audio recorder on the researchers smartphone.

Since the focus group could not be conducted in the environments themselves, photographs of each room were used as memory probes. This visual aid helped participants recall specific sensory details and experiences from each environment, facilitating a more detailed and accurate discussion (Latham, assumption was not met, transformations were tried. If they did not improve the normality, a Mixed model would have been performed, as they are more robust.

The psychological stress was also analysed with sensory appraisal as predictor. For this a Linear Mixed Model was performed, accounting for repeated measurements using participant ID as random intercept.
These models were tested for the normality of the residuals assumption using the Shapiro-Wilk test, homoskedasticity using visual inspection of a residual vs fitted scatterplot.

div.head: Physiology
div.p: The raw heart rate variability (HRV) data was downloaded from PhyLo (after being measured with the Mobi 8 device) and analysed using Kubios HRV Scientific 4.1.1, a validated software for HRV processing. Artefacts and noise in RR intervals were automatically corrected and manually checked based on established guidelines. with noise detection set to medium, and the beat correction on the standard 0.3 (Lipponen & Tarvainen, 2019). Detected ectopic beats and abnormal RR intervals were corrected through interpolation, ensuring data integrity (Lipponen & Tarvainen, 2019). Noise segments were disregarded from the analysis. Samples with more than 5% corrected beats or more than 5% noise were excluded. This has led to the exclusion of 1 participant data, (for all rooms, all samples) and one extra sample. RMSSD values falling outside the healthy range (6.9-99.4 ms; Agelink et al., 1998) were also excluded, which has led to the exclusion of three rooms for 1 participant, and four other samples.

HRV was analysed in three five-minute time bins (5-10 min, 25-30 min, 45-50 min). Mean RMSSD per condition was compared to all three of the psychological stress dimensions by means of linear mixed model. Furthermore, a mean RMSSD effect was analysed as dependent variable for effects by the predictor room manipulations by means of a repeated Anova. This model is also tested on the assumptions of normality of. A linear mixed model was run to investigate the effect of sensory appraisal on the mean RMSSD, with ID as random intercept to account for the repeated measurements. To check the RMSSD progression throughout the working hour, the three time bins will be assessed visually, for possible stress restoration or progression.

div.head: Sensory appraisals and psycho-physiological stress analysis
div.p: Psychological stress Tension A linear mixed-effects model was conducted to examine the relationship between Tension as dependent variable and the predictors smell appraisal and touch appraisal, while accounting for repeated measurements using a random intercept for ID. It was run with robust standard errors, adjusting for clustering within participants, as the normality assumption was not met (Swilk-test p = 0.007). The overall model was found statistically significant with a Chi2 = 57.49 (p < 0.001).

The analysis revealed a significant negative effect of smell appraisal on tension (β = -2.29, SE = 0.85, z = -2.68, p = 0.01), indicating that more positive ratings of smell were associated with lower tension.

Similarly, touch appraisal also had a significant negative effect on tension (β = -2.63, SE = 1.14, z = -2.30, p = 0.02), suggesting that a more positive rating were linked to lower tension. These two effects are visualised in figure 13. The interaction effect between smell and touch appraisal showed a nonsignificant trend (β = 0.35, SE = 0.18, z = 1.94, p = 0.053), indicating that there is no strong evidence that the effect of smell appraisal on tension depended on touch appraisal (or vice versa). Overall, these results suggest that both smell and touch contribute to reduced Tension.

div.head: Pleasure
div.p: A linear mixed-effects model was run for the dependent variable pleasure was well, also while accounting for repeated measurements by random intercept for ID. This model too was run robust, as it did not meet the assumptions of normality (Swilk-test p = 0.01). The overall model fit was found to be statistically significant with Chi2 = 38.93 (p = 0.00).

The model showed a statistically significant effect for both the smell appraisal (β = 1.79, SE = 0.34, z = 5.26, p = 0.00), as for the touch appraisal (β = 2.25, SE = 0.42, z = 5.40, p = 0.00) on pleasure. Both positive coefficients indicate that a higher rating of smell or touch correlate with a higher rating of pleasure. The interaction between smell and touch appraisal too was found to be statistically significant (β = -0.30, SE = 0.06, z = -4.68, p = 0.00), indicating that the relationship between smell appraisal and pleasure depends on the value of touch appraisal (or vice versa). Specifically, the negative coefficient suggests that as touch appraisal increases, the effect of smell appraisal on pleasure becomes less positive (or more negative). This effect is showcased in figure 14. The first graph shows when touch is rated 1, a more positive appraisal of smell increases pleasure, but in the second and third graph, when touch appraisal increases, the starting point of pleasure (with low smell appraisal), is already high, and therefore flattens out.

div.head: Awake
div.p: To investigate the effect of the smell and touch appraisal on the awake dimension, another Linear Mixed Model was run with ID as random intercept. The residuals followed a normal distribution (Swilk-test p = 0.11). The overall model was found not to be statistically significant with Chi2 = 5.87, p = 0.12.

The analysis found no statistically significant effects for smell appraisal (β =1.91, SE = 1.05, z = 1.82, p = 0.07), nor for touch appraisal (β = 1.53, SE = 1.25, z = 1.22, p = 0.22). Also the interaction effect was found not to be statistically significant (β = -0.31, SE = 0.23, z = -1.32, p = 0.19). This means that the data did not find any evidence for an effect of touch or smell appraisal and feeling awake, nor that the two sensory appraisals influenced each other's effect on the awake rating.

div.head: Physiological stress
div.p: To test for an effect of the touch and smell appraisal on the mean RMSSD (physiological stress), another linear mixed model was run, with ID as random intercept. This model too was run robust as it did not meet the normality assumption (Swilk-test p = 0.01). The overall model was reported to be not statistically significant with a Chi2 = 2.86, p = 0.41.

The model found no statistically significant correlation for smell appraisal (β =-1.07, SE = 2.32, z = -0.46, p = 0.64), nor for the touch appraisal (β =3.04, SE = 4.03, z = 0.75, p = 0.45). Also the interaction effect was found not to be significant (β =-0.13, SE = 0.51, z = , p = 0.07). This indicates that the model did not find any evidence for an effect of touch or smell appraisal on the mean RMSSD and thus physiological stress, nor that the two sensory appraisals influenced each other's effect on the awake rating.

div.head: mediation analysis
div.p: The previous analyses have shown that there is no statistically significant effect for path a nor for path c (see figure 6, chapter 3.6). Therefore, a mediation analysis is not necessary, as there is no indication of a mediation effect.
