The qualitative analysis of the interviews and focus groups provides insights into how participants perceived and experienced the experimental conditions. The applied coding framework and the frequency of occurrences can be found in Appendix H. The transcripts were kept in the same language as the interview or focus group was in (English and Dutch, depending on whether everyone in the group spoke Dutch). The snippets in the results have been translated to English. Where translations might not have precisely the same connotation, the original wording is presented as well.
Theme 1: Smell experience 1.1 Smell strength perception varies among participants Participants perceived smells differently depending on their sensitivity and positioning within the space.
The same scent was sometimes unnoticed by one participant but perceived as too strong by another.

Smell was more likely to go unnoticed if it was introduced in the first room participants entered, and scents tended to fade from awareness over time. 'I remember thinking that it didn't completely smell like nothing like the other room. The other room which had no smell, I assume. So I remember smelling that it was a little bit different. But I couldn't like, honestly, if I didn't. If I wasn't in the room with absolutely no smell before, I probably would have said that it smelled like nothing, so.'(p9)

div.head: The smell appraisal through personal association
div.p: The smell was often described as homely or like a 'department/home-goods or fragrance' store. These personal associations could influence the experience of the scent, ' When I'm at my parents' home, there is always a scented candle lit. Or the fireplace is lit in the winter. So I am really used to strong scents being present. So I thought it was rather nice. I only thought, I'm studying at my parents place' (p3) as well as the experience of the room 'I really think that a room is more cosy (Dutch: gezellig) with the scent present'( p7). Although this relaxed association was not loved by all participants in the particular setting 'I think it is also a bit distracting. Or maybe… It can be positively distracting, like it makes you more relaxed. But that is not really appropriate' (p13). These associations also had those effects in a more negative point of view. 'It smelled a little musty. First of all, it is not nice to enter a musty room. Secondly, it also makes you drowsy and tired (Dutch: Muffen en inkakken) as well'(p1).

div.head: The smell appraisal through smell strength
div.p: When participants rated a scent positively, they described it as just "nice," whereas negative ratings were often strongly unfavourable. 'When you don't smell anything, that is super positive. Because you don't experience any negative.. I'm thinking, when it comes to smell, when you don't notice it, it is good.

Because there is nothing stinky or distracting, especially when studying.'(p7). It was quite apparent that the absence of the smell was also rated as positive, as well as a slight scent that would tune out over time. 'I don't mind the smell. It was just like something I noticed but it kind of went away in a bit. I kind of got used to it quickly, so.' (p15). Yet, when the scent was experienced as very strong, people had more issues with tuning it out, 'It was a nice smell, but it was very present. It was so strong I could not get used to it' (p7), and often experienced it as more negative 'I really couldn't handle the scent. It really was not for me.' (p4) To even physical discomforts 'it was so strong that I can feel it itching in my nose. ' (p9).
Theme 2: Touch experience 2.1 Physical touch, the joys of softness and annoyance of slippery items

The physical touch aspects participants reported on, were mainly the items around the desk. Soft textures were generally experience positively, especially the blanket on the chair. 'The blanket on the chair, in the first room I didn't use it. I was already very warm, so I didn't need it. But I liked having something on my lap. It was like a soothing behaviour for me (p3). But also without intent interaction, they liked having a soft blanket in their back 'When it hit my back, I thought ooohh nice soft blanket' (p6). Also the softness of the table cloth was sometimes rated positive 'the cloth on the table was nice.

In a very simple way, because it is softer... when you place your arm on the edge of the desk the whole time, because of the laptop, it is not on a hard edge the whole time. (p11). Yet, some also experienced the tablecloth as annoying, mostly due to the slippery movement 'I thought the tablecloth was very annoying. Because when your laptop was on it, and it moved around.. It was also placed over cables which made that it wasn't laying down straight. …. Something should not distract, something that moves when I move. For example a mousepad would have been fine, that doesn't move when I move my mouse.

(p6). Also the size of the desk varied from the soft rooms (smaller) than in the hard rooms, which was noted. Smaller desks were experienced as more annoying 'That desk was very small. I'm a person that uses both laptop and an iPad. And then I also have my water and a keyboard with me. (p3) 2.2 Embodied touch appraisal and other visual aspects Many of the visual aspects in the room were placed outside of the participants reach, but were still experienced through embodied touch. 'So in a way, there was less that I physically touched, but more the 'Oh I could nicely lay in the couch and that would feel nice'(p1). Especially the couch was often mentioned and talked about looking comfortable. This embodied experience was also sometimes confirmed 'it looked like it could be comfortable. When I tried it out, it was comfortable. (p15 about the couch). This embodied experience already started when entering the room, giving a very quick sense of the room 'I knew I walked inside and saw, I thought, O how nice, a blanket! (p5). Another visually haptic aspect mentioned was the feel and structure of the space, especially concerning the table cloth.

Whether this was positive 'It was kind of nice to for example place some other stuff on it (the table cloth) or make a bit of a distinction in your workplace' (p11) Or negative 'Maybe it also takes up space visually, from your whole desk.' (p5). The visual embodiment of the touch experience mostly led to atmospheric experiences through personal associations.

div.head: Touch appraisal and personal associations and emotions
div.p: Softness was commonly associated with a homely atmosphere, often through simulated touch. It frequently gave a positive feeling and experience, 'I thought the warm rooms also felt warmer. You are more at ease there'(p7 about soft environment) Or it even made them feel more safe 'It feels safe when there is a couch with stuffed animals on it' (p3).. This could also evoke feelings of relaxation or even the urge to lie down or take a break or even a nap, which was sometimes reported on as positive 'It makes it very homely. I get more motivated by it, because then I see a couch and I think 'Oh, I could lie on that when I'm done'' (p10), but also sometimes as inappropriate for a work/study setting or demotivating 'This (relaxing behaviour) is associated with the environment (soft room), so you are more easily inclined to relax and maybe work a little less hard (p11)'. Also, the direct feeling of softness, for example of the blanket, was associated with homely and relaxing surroundings 'At home I also often take an extra pillow on my lap. I don't know, it just feels nice. So, when I'm at home it is the first thing I do, I think it is just relaxing. (p3). But in that focus group conversation others commented, this soothing homely association had also been experienced as inappropriate for the setting 'I think it is lovely too, but not when I'm studying. The I know I just don't want to study anymore, get cosy underneath a blanket (p7). The hard environment on the other hand, although less talked about in terms of touch, had more associations with office like environments. This touch experience was not always met as positive 'It felt very static and cold' (p7). A few participants, mostly female, mentioned feeling cold, which they found distracting.

Theme 3 : Stress 3.1 Calmness induced by the rooms Stress was not often explicitly mentioned by participants. Instead, feelings of calmness and relaxation were noted more frequently, which is often regarded as the opposite. 'For me it (soft furnishing) was the first thing I noticed. And that was the first thing that brought me rest. I immediately had a feeling of peace (Dutch: rust)' (p3 on soft room). Which was earlier also mentioned in the soft homely warm associations of the soft rooms, as well as with the soothing behaviour of the blanket on the lap. 'Concerning productivity I didn't feel the rooms made much of a difference. But I did notice it being more chill in the soft rooms. Again with the idea that it is more atmospheric' (p10). Even though the participants did mention relaxing feelings towards some of the room design elements, they often were sceptical about whether the environment could induce stress. Participants used more positive wording, but when asked directly about stress, most responses suggested annoyance or lack of focus rather than acute stress. The word stress seemed too strong to use. 'Maybe because I didn't have any real stressful activity today. Productivity maybe a little bit, but that was more… for me it was more clear that that was because it was the end of the day (p1 when asked about his stress).

div.head: Stressing factors
div.p: Although, the word stress was not often attributed by the participants, the cases when stronger negative emotions were communicated, it was mostly due to the smell being too strong, but strong wording was hardly ever mentioned. 'Room 1 is the bottom one for me, because I really couldn't handle the scent'(p4). Also, for the table cloth, some annoyance was mentioned 'And I thought the tablecloth was terribly annoying, laying on the table'(p6. Yet, when asked whether this was stress inducing, or they felt more stress in this room, they mentioned not to feel that much stress or were sceptical whether the stress was induced by the room, but attribute it more to other factors such as their activity 'Researcher: I'm interested in your stress levels, can you elaborate on how they were and how they might have differed per room? P4: My stress is generally low as I only have one course at the moment… Only in the 4 th room I was reading a super exciting suspenseful chapter of a book which might have made me stressed' or attributed stress to frustration towards themselves due to a lack of focus ' In room 4 (soft, no smell) I thought, I'm stuck. So I noticed to get more stressed, because I thought I really have to get on with it' (p10). The personal association of the room also was mentioned to induce irritation indirectly 'The I think, no, well shit, why can't I do it there (on focussing in the hard room)? Then I get a little irritated more quickly. But I think that I conditioned myself that I have to perform well in bare (Dutch: kale) rooms.' (p3) 4: Other Findings 4.1 Effort put in the room is positive Some participants elaborated that effort being put in the environment has for them a positive effect, mediating a more positive experience of an environment. If I were to relate this to somewhere outside, I would also feel like, yeah, I do appreciate it when people at least make an effort to make the space nice. If you have one of those awful office spaces, you might as well do something with it. (p1)This can be in multiple forms. In this pilot has both been said about the scent as the decorations in the soft rooms 'Precisely when there is a scent, you know that some attention has been given to it, and that the room will make you feel a bit more comfortable because you know that some effort has been put into it" (p.11).

div.head: Individual differences in positive stimulation or distraction
div.p: There seemed to be individual differences in preference for distractions were evident: while some required a plain, minimalistic environment to focus, or even the personal association of an office, others needed slight stimuli to avoid becoming distracted by larger disruptions. For example, 'I found all the decorations in the rooms to be really distracting while studying. And in the basically empty rooms, I was. I could really focus really well' (p9). Meanwhile, the other participant in this focus group argued 'Because just studying in an empty room with absolutely nothing interesting to see while doing, like, very, you know, not particularly, like, you know, vibrant work, just, like, reading and taking notes and all that. And also just in dead silence, my mind was screaming for anything. Like, any kind of stimulus. So when I was actually, more comfortable in rooms that I had some stuff to look at or actually nice smells, it did feel a bit better.' (p15). This need for stimulation was even more sought after in the context of working there for longer period than an hour '"So for your psyche, I would say it's better than spending the whole day in a bare room where you're just staring at a white wall or a white pillar" (p.11). Homely associations elicited mixed responses-some found them calming, while others felt they hindered productivity by making them too relaxed, as also discussed in the previous sections.

div.head: seating arrangements induced social cues
div.p: Seating arrangements also influenced perceptions; soft and well-used chairs were often seen as social spaces, which was generally viewed positively. ´In the other two rooms (soft rooms), it actually felt like, you know, like someone actually, you know, worked there or studied there. Someone actually took the effort' (p15). This social cue also seemed to be influenced by the arrangement of the seatings 'I found it really strange if I didn't take care of this, but basically, the chairs were positioned in such a way that it really looked like two people had just gotten up. (p4) R: okay, and was that a positive or negative thing? P4: Yeah, kind of like that cozy, homely feeling that you recognize, you know? It just gives a good feeling. Yeah, okay." 4.4 A need for balance and variety in environments Several participants emphasized the need for balance or a change in scenery depending on their work tasks. '"I think, on the one hand, that I do like having an environment where you can work well. But I think it's more about having a bit of variety that's good. And also, that you associate that variety with the space you're in. So, for example, if I say, okay, I've worked for an hour, I want to take a 15-minute break. Then, ideally, I would leave a somewhat plainer room to go to a warmer environment for a while.

div.head: And vice versa, if I've just had my break in a cozy space, I would then go back to a slightly plainer room to continue working." (p11)
div.p: While proprioception and ergonomics were occasionally mentioned in conversation as a remark on the room, they fell outside the scope of this pilot study.

div.head: Quantitative results
div.p: None of the room conditions (smell or soft materiality) showed to have any statistically significant effect on either one of the psychological stress dimensions, nor the physiological stress mean RMSSD.

The physiological stress (RMSSD) unexpectedly correlated negatively with the tension dimension, indicating that higher tension would be correlated with lower physiological stress. The room manipulations, smell and soft, also showed not to be statistically significantly correlated with the sensory appraisals of smell or touch (/feel). The trajectory seems to show a declining physiological stress over the time spent in the room, for 3 of the 4 rooms. Yet, this is not statistically analysed.

The only statistically significant findings this quantitative analysis did find was on the effect of the sensory appraisals of both smell and touch on the psychological stress dimensions tension and pleasure, indicating more positive appraisals showing lower tension and higher pleasure. The interaction of smell and touch appraisal also was statistically significant for pleasure, indicating that the relationship between smell appraisal and pleasure depends on the value of touch appraisal (or vice versa).

Specifically, the negative coefficient suggests that as touch appraisal increases, the effect of smell appraisal on pleasure becomes less positive (or more negative). The dimension awake or physiological stress (RMSSD) did not show significant effects.
As two of the three paths, as per the mediation diagram, were not statistically significant, there is no indication of any mediation. Therefore, a mediation analysis was not performed.

div.head: Qualitative analysis
div.p: Smell played a significant role in how participants perceived their environment, through perception, personal association and strength. The presence of a distinct scent was sometimes associated with care and intentionality or comforting personal associations. Yet it could also have very negative effects when the scent was too strong and/or disliked. The negative effects seemed more impactful than the positive.
Also, the absence of any (bad) smell was considered positive.

Touch and texture were also important factors in shaping participants' experiences. Soft and comfortable elements were often preferred over hard, plane surfaces, as they contributed to a sense of relaxation and comfort. Yet this was not always appreciated. Some felt that that association was not appropriate or were a bit annoyed by distractions or moving elements.
A key theme was the psychological effects of different environments, particularly in relation to stress.

Stress was not often mentioned; participants talked more about calmness (the positive opposite) or used less strong words such as annoyance. The calmness was mostly related to the soft and warm environments. Possible stressors were strong smells, their inability to focus (while being in a room/setting where one is ought to focus), or their own tasks. This was not often contributed to the room. Whereas the positive calmness was noted to be linked with the environment.

There were some additional findings such as the positive effect of the idea that someone put thought in an environment, the need for variation in the work environment throughout a day, the positive notes of traces of human presence, and the big individual differences in over-or under stimulation of an environment.

Overall, the analysis suggests that participants have very different opinions and needs for a working environment for various reasons. This could conclude in their appreciation for an environment that balances functionality with warmth or a variation of space throughout their day, depending on their activity.

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: This thesis work made use of a wide arrangement of methodologies, to learn how sensory ethnographic methodologies could add additional insights on workplace research, more specifically concerning psycho-physiological stress in relation to touch and smell. The strength of this study is that it used both quantitative techniques to measure effects, and qualitative ethnographic techniques to find explanations and context of the effects found in the quantitative data. This study was performed with an explorative nature, as these methodologies are not often combined, and these sensory modalities are not often researched in the physical workplace environment. This exploration has provided some interesting insights in both the effects and mechanisms of the sensory influence on psycho-physiological stress, and in employing sensory ethnographic and physiological techniques in workplace research. Key findings include: (1) the liking/appraisal of smell and touch is highly subjective, but plays a big role in psycho-physiological stress, (2) homely associations may lead to (too much) restoration, (3) The touch experience does not have to be physical but can be visually simulated, (4) Accurately conducting and interpreting physiological stress measurements presents considerable methodological challenges, and (5) there seems to be a dissonance in performing ethnography in a lab setting. After, these discussion points have been explained, the main learning goal of ( 6) what can we learn about applying ethnographic methods in workplace design and psycho-physiological stress can be discussed.

div.head: The role of touch and smell appraisal
div.p: The findings of this study underscore the importance of sensory appraisal-the way individuals interpret sensory stimuli-in shaping psychological stress responses. While the room manipulations (smell and soft materiality) showed no direct effect on psycho-physiological stress, participants' subjective experiences of these stimuli did relate to psychological stress dimensions, particularly tension and pleasure. These results showed more positive appraisals correlating with lower tension and higher pleasure. This highlights that it is not just the presence of touch and smell alone, but how they are perceived and appraised may also determine their impact.

As supported by previous literature (Bentley et al., 2022;Matsubara et al., 2023;Spence, 2020b), sensory experiences are highly personal and context-dependent. This was echoed in the qualitative data: participants rated the same sensory environment in vastly different ways, often grounded in personal associations. Spence (2020b) explains this as a very common mechanisms, where people place positive or negative associations on smells through associative learning through earlier experiences. Although the citrus scent was chosen based on literature suggesting its general pleasantness (Liu et al., 2023;Spence, 2020b), participants' responses ranged from feeling comforted to distracted or demotivatedwith ranging associations such as 'homely settings by the fireplace', 'baking cookies' or 'department stores', all experiences participant are likely to have learned to associate the smells with through memory or culturalization (Spence, 2020b). Similarly, the soft materiality elicited both relaxation and discomfort, depending on whether participants associated it with a cozy home or an unfitting work atmosphere. These findings align with research showing that touch perception is also influenced by prior experience and context (Crippa et al., 2012;Plaisier et al., 2023), though literature on the link between touch and stress remains limited. As these experiences can be very much variating between different people, workplace designers might want to refrain from using very strong sensory features such as a strong smell. Sticking to more neutral, and generally positively associated cues could be a more appropriate course.

The empirical study findings suggesting that positively rated sensory inputs can reduce psychological stress, are corroborated by literature (Liu et al., 2023;Matsubara et al., 2023;Spence, 2020b). However, no associations were found between sensory input and physiological stress (RMSSD), which was unexpected given that other research did find evidence linking pleasant scents with HRV (e.g. Liu et al., 2023). A possible explanation, besides the small sample size, is that this study only used RMSSD as a physiological marker, which may also reflect cognitive load, fatigue or arousal (Srinivasan et al., 2024). Higher levels of fatigue as well as arousal are typically linked to decreased RMSSD values, indicating reduced parasympathetic activity and a heightened physiological stress response (Huo et al., 2023;Srinivasan et al., 2024). Moreover, it is good to note that physiological stress often finds low consistency over different studies (Schuller, in press) and psychological and physiological stress often show weak correlations (Ginty et al., 2017).

div.head: Homely associations and (too much) restoration
div.p: The study found that the soft environments, and the smell created homely associations for many of the participants. As Chatterjee (2021) explained, the participants described in the focus groups how the smells, soft textures or furnishing reminded them of similar experiences in home environments, creating homely associations. They reported to feel more at rest and calm in those environments, especially concerning the soft materiality. Other studies, too, seemed to find similar effects. Graham et al. (2015), suggest that environments emphasizing comfort, togetherness, and intimacy can significantly reduce stress and improve mood by providing a sense of security and emotional support. But what their study also found is that this need varied per room that they studied. For instance, home offices and study areas, designed for productivity and stimulation, were found to enhance focus and concentration. The ambiance in these rooms is tailored to support cognitive tasks and minimize distractions, thereby improving concentration and academic performance (Graham, Gosling, & Travis, 2015). This also reads into the findings from the focus groups. Many participants reported feeling calmer and at rest in the rooms described as 'homely', yet what some of them also reported is how they did not like that for the specific context of a working/study area. They felt less focussed, less productive which could in some cases then again increase stress or annoyance. This effect can also be explained by the Yerkes-Dodson law (1908), which posits that there is an optimal level of arousal (stress and alertness) for peak performance. According to this law, moderate levels of stress can enhance focus and productivity, while too little or too much stress can impair performance. This inverted-U relationship suggests that a certain amount of stress is necessary to maintain alertness and motivation, but excessive stress can lead to burnout and decreased productivity (Cohen, 2011;Yerkes & Dodson, 1908). When the stress becomes too excessive, it becomes problematic, but too much restoration is not fitting for a workplace context.

A workplace should try to facilitate that optimum level of arousal for employees to be able to focus and be productive. The focus groups of the empirical study also mentioned that the feeling of focus and productivity in that setting, is positive for their overall mood and subjective wellbeing. The workplace environment should therefore not be a stressor, but should also not have too much stress restoration effect, for example via homely associations. What those exact design aspects are, are again based on personal associations and should be researched more.

div.head: The role of embodied touch
div.p: In the empirical study, the soft environments were also decorated with soft textures that the participants did not physically touch. Still they did mention for instance how the couch looked comfortable or how they looked forward to touching the blanket in the chair as it looked soft. Spence (2020a) also mentions that the tactile element is important, whether an object is touched or not. He states that material choices can evoke a sense of tactility, as the viewer or occupant mentally simulates the sensation of touching or caressing a visually engaging surface (Gallese, 2017;Spence, 2020a). It is interesting to see how this simulated touch, could still evoke emotions and could maybe also be stress reducing. This study did not particularly set out to measure these simulated effects, but they did emerge in the focus group conversations and seemed to have played a role in the experience of materiality. Ebisch et al. (2008) also showed neurological similarities between touch observations and being touched themselves, especially in intended touch. It might also be interesting to look into the relation with the 'look and feel' aspects of office design, which is researched more often (Al Horr et al., 2016;Kropman et al., 2023).

When look and feel are described they are mostly described as visual aspects such as aesthetics, but the embodied touch might play a role in this. This was also proposed by Gallese (2017Gallese ( , 2019)), where he argues that embodied simulation offers a fresh perspective on aesthetic experience and can be considered an interesting link in bridging neuroscience and the humanities within the biocultural framework. These ideas now mainly stem from artistic practices and ideas (Gallese, 2017;Hayes & Rajko, 2017) but could be interesting to investigate how they might translate into workplace design.

These ideas call for more cross modal and multisensory research and design approaches (Spence, 2020a), also investigating the interaction of the senses and how they might play a role in aesthetics and ambiance.

div.head: Challenges in Measuring Physiological Stress
div.p: This empirical study found some unusual findings concerning the physiological stress data. Not only did it not find any statistically significant effects with any of the predictors, even where psychological stress did, it even had a negative relation with psychological stress. This would indicate that the higher the psychological stress, the lower the physiological stress. It is not too strange that psychological stress and physiological stress show different results, although interlinked they are distinct concepts (Ginty et al., 2017), but the negative relation with psychological stress seems irregular. This thesis showed that there is a need for expertise to perform physiological measurements well and reliably. A lack in expertise and confounding factors could lead to less reliable and accurate results (Schuller, in press).

The study found that the analysis process itself too is very time consuming and requires expertise to do well. Furthermore a highly controlled study was necessary for reliable data, due to many probable confounding factors. These can be both difficult to acquire in 'real setting' workplace research, but necessary for reliable results. Many other papers too seem to struggle to find good quality, consistent and replicable physiological stress measurements in workplace design (Schuller, in press). She, for instance, argues that there is a growing interest in wearable physiology measurement equipment, but workplace researchers should be mindful of the complex biological nature of physiological stress and the limitations of applying physiological measures in real-world settings. Although tools like HRV and EDA could be well-suited for field research, their reliability can be compromised by confounding factors present outside controlled environments (Schuller, in press). Although HRV and EDA are one of the most used measurement techniques for physiological stress (Valentine, 2023), it might also be of interest to investigate other measurement types such as blood pressure, respiratory rate or body temperature (Valentine, 2023). Yet, it could very well be the case that these methodologies would propose similar difficulties because of the highly complex biology (Schuller, in press). The ethnographic methods could possibly help explain certain context for possible effects or lack of effects, this is probably more the case for psychological stress. As discussed in the literature review, physiological stress can is not always experienced consciously (Becker et al., 2023). This is why physiological measurements done reliably and well, is still very important.

5.5 The dissonance of ethnography in a lab setting and how to balance Ethnography, as described in the literature section, is where the researcher also immerses themselves in the experience and tries to research the real and direct environment and sensory experiences (Pink, 2015). Performing ethnography in a lab setting is therefore inherently contradictory. This lab setting was purposely chosen to still be able to manipulate the environment, to investigate certain sensory modalities, without other confounding factors and to help the physiology measurements. Other controls such as prohibiting coffee intake and semi controlling for tasks, were necessary for gaining more reliable physiological data in this lab setting. This too is in contrast with the ethnographic ideology and might infringe on the ecological validity. But it reflects on the difficult and nuanced balance of trying to marry the two methodologies. In future research this balance should be considered well and formed accordingly to the main research objective.

Also, this study did not take the researcher as first person perspective, but merely analysed the participants responses alone. Although, this, as well as the combination of more quantitative measurements, has been done more often under the title of ethnographic methods (Bolger et al., 2003;Clarkson & Hodgkinson, 1999;Mazzola et al., 2011;Warren, 2002), whether it really is ethnography in the first essential definition might be debatable. It did work out well to take the participants perspective as main perspective, as the data showed a wide variety of experiences and personal associations and opinions. This might not have been as clearly shown if the researchers first perspective would have been the main perspective and could therefore be a good approach in highly subjective experiences. The researcher was still involved in the environment and experience, in the sense that the researcher designed the environment to their (and the supervisors) interpretation of what soft and hard environments would constitute of, and what scent would be nice and appropriate. This resulted in a subjectively designed environment, engaging the researcher in an ethnographic sense. This was also done in earlier work-place ethnographic studies (Warren, 2002(Warren, , 2008)). The environment design was based on the researchers own experiences, which was then in the empirical study reflected on by the participants. Although most of them let know that they knew that the researcher designed it, they did not seem to have difficulty expressing critiques on the environment. This could be due to the student knowledge that it was university equipment, or that experimental environment manipulations often do not per say reflect the opinions and likings of the researcher, but are based on the study's research aim.
Another way the researcher was involved in the ethnographic process was via the subjectivity in coding.
Although, it was tried to perform the coding and thematic analysis as objective as possible, it is very difficult to refrain from any subjectivity in that process.

div.head: What can sensory-ethnographic methods add to workplace design research?
div.p: From the literature review was learned that ethnographic methods has been applied in workplace design research (Warren, 2002) and workplace stress (McGibbon et al., 2010;Soucek et al., 2023), but not often in sensory sense and not often combined with psycho-physiological stress. Yet, there did seem to be indications that it could have potentially interesting insights to combine these quantitative and qualitative measurements (Mazzola et al., 2011;Soucek et al., 2023).

Previously, stress was often not a main research goal in sensory ethnographic research, especially concerning workplace design, but it did sometimes came up as a topic (Clarkson & Hodgkinson, 1999;Glaw et al., 2017;Golvani et al., 2021). This thesis learned that you could use it as main topic and research it more focussed, but does call for keeping the conversations open to context and nuance, as that is the main strength of sensory ethnography (Pink, 2015). As established before, the combination with physiological stress might be more difficult to perform in workplace research. Although it would have been interesting to be able to get the quantitative and qualitative data really side by side, this might prove to be difficult. This thesis did find a novel way how the data could enrich each other none the less. The ethnographic methods were able to provide rich context, reflexivity and highlighted mechanisms of psycho-physiological stress effects based on. This was already speculated based on the literature review where it was applied in different context and research goals (Pink, 2013), and confirmed in this domain as well.

Diaries, while already known for capturing in situ information (Bolger et al., 2003;Reid et al., 2011), also proved to be valuable tools as probes in the mediated focus groups, prompting reflection and memory during interviews. They could enhance the depth of insights and help the researcher structure focus groups better, with more targeted questions. This method could therefore possibly be considered both effective and easy to use for workplace research, especially when combined with interviews and focus groups. Regarding diary questions, literature shows a mix of open and more directed formats (Bolger et al., 2003;Mazzola et al., 2011;Reid et al., 2011). For lesser-explored senses, more guided questions might be more effective, as the more open questions often led to vague or visually-biased responses. In both real-world and lab workplace settings, participants could benefit from some guidance to access and articulate subtle sensory experiences that may not be top-of-mind (Pink, 2015).

In the literature review, it was established that an important part of sensory ethnography is trying to gather the information in situ, while experiencing the sensory encounters (Pink, 2015). Yet, this might not always be possible in certain settings or experiment designs. This study has showcased, that although it is important to direct the participants to the sensory modalities and experiences, recalling it aided by visual prompts and embodied experiences (Gallese, 2017) can still provide very valuable insights and still help participants recall and explain their experience. This is where the ethnographic method could really add to the more traditional methods, by guiding the participants through their sensory experiences. This seems especially key when researching lesser consciously experienced senses such as touch and smell. Although this method did not guide the participants as much as for example in smellwalks (Low, 2015;Pink, 2015;Sparkes, 2009), but it was already noticed that the open-ended, not sensory steered questions, were very visually or ambiance focussed. The more sensory focussed questions already seemed to help guiding the participants, but the most insightful information was gathered in the focus groups, where the most guidance, directed questions and follow-up questions would be asked.

All in all, the ethnographic methods of diaries and focus groups/interviews did seem very applicable and appropriate, for lab settings but also for in situ workplace studies. How the balance should be in lab setting vs in situ setting depends on the specific research goal. The lab setting can uncover more specific effects and can be more easily controlled which is especially practical with physiological measurements, whereas in situ research can give higher ecological validity. This holds especially true for senses that are less actively consciously experienced, such as touch and smell. It revealed how sensory stimuli are interpreted through personal associations, how "homely" design elements can both calm and distract, and how even visually simulated touch may shape experiences. Together, these findings support the value of incorporating sensory ethnographic methodologies in workplace research, especially when studying subtle and subjective phenomena like sensory modalities and stress.

div.head: Limitations
div.p: This study provided valuable insights into the impact of sensory environments on psycho-physiological stress, yet several limitations should be noted. The biggest limitation was the small sample size, which resulted in potentially lower reliability and smaller chances of finding statistically significant effects.

Secondly, the environmental conditions were not fully controlled: visual stimulation differed between rooms, one room was noted to be affected by external noise, and the "no-smell" condition may have been compromised by a reported musty odour. These inconsistencies may have influenced participants' experiences and affected the clarity of the manipulations. The environmental set-up was also based on rather limited existing insights and mostly the opinion of the researcher (and supervisors). This could have led to less optimal staging, and a bigger variance in appraisal of the conditions. In terms of physiological measurements, as mentioned in the discussion, HRV analysis required significant expertise, particularly in preprocessing and interpretation, and the use of only RMSSD limited the nuance of stress assessment. EDA data was excluded due to lack of time and expertise, as well as probable data noise caused by hand movements. Strict controls over participant behaviour, such as restrictions on caffeine or music, were necessary for physiological reliability but reduced ecological validity. Similarly, conducting all conditions in one day introduced potential fatigue or order effects, which randomization could not fully eliminate-especially given the small sample size. But this was also necessary to control for daily variances in psycho-physiological stress. This study also did not take sensory interactions into account in the measurements, even though the results and other work suggests that this might play a role in the environment experience.

div.head: Future research recommendations
div.p: There is still a lot unknown in how different senses influence the psycho-physiological stress in the physical workplace. Future studies that mean to combine ethnographic techniques and quantitative measurements like this study, should first clearly define their main research objective and adjust the balance between controlled lab setting and ethnography with ecological validity accordingly. There should be a better investigation how physiological measurements can be applied more reliably in the workplace setting. Furthermore, pre-testing sensory elements-such as scent intensity and pleasantness-could ensure more consistent and positive experiences across participants, while involving users or design experts in defining environmental qualities like "softness" can reduce subjective bias. From the discussion we learned that homely associations have effect on calmness or could even lead to too much calmness. Interesting research would be what design attributes make for a homely environment, and what the optimal level of 'homeliness' and restoration would be for an office environment. This could also be studied in how it differs per room function, such as an office, meeting room or break room. Also, multisensory and cross-modal research could help gaining a better understanding in how we experience the workplace environment, for example with simulated touch or sensory congruency.

div.head: Implications for practice
div.p: This study illustrates the importance of considering a broader range of sensory factors-beyond the visual and acoustic-when designing workplace environments. Elements like material softness, ambient scent, and embodied, haptic experiences can all shape how people feel and function in a space. However, workplace design should strike a careful balance: while spaces that can help restore and reduce too much job stress, spaces that are too stress-reducing due to too much homeliness and/or softness, might not be appropriate either. This could potentially diminish focus, alertness, or productivity. It could be a good idea to make differentiation in different rooms with different functions. This would also help in the fact that the effects the environment can have are highly individual and subjective. If possible, giving employees an option in what kind of environment to work in, provides them a sense of control and can help them find their own optimal level of restoration and stimulation.

Concerning smell, it was found that the absence of smell was already rated as highly positive. Artificial smells, even 'nice smells', can be experienced very differently. When experienced as negative, the effect on their mood seems to be highly negative. Concerning touch, design decisions should move beyond surface-level aesthetics or technical functionality and start to consider materiality in a more holistic way-how materials feel, how they are experienced physically or embodied, and how they influence perception and emotion. There is still much to uncover about the complex interactions between sensory design, cognition, and stress, particularly regarding less-studied senses like smell and touch. These findings advocate for a more multisensory and human-centred approach to workplace design that recognizes the nuanced and individual ways people experience their environments.

how sensory ethnography can enhance research on workplace design and psychophysiological stress by focusing on the underexplored senses of smell and touch. The literature study found that there is already quite a body of work concerning visual and acoustic influences, but smell and touch, although possibly showing promise of influence on the psycho-physiological stress levels of employees, has not been researched as much. The empirical study highlighted that smell and touch design might influence psychological stress, but primarily through personal sensory appraisal of the sensory experience rather than direct sensory input-highlighting the importance of subjective interpretation. The literature and the study demonstrated that sensory ethnographic techniques, such as sensory diaries and focus groups, can effectively capture nuanced, in-the-moment experiences of smell and touch. However, these have rarely been integrated with physiological measures like HRV, which proved difficult to perform as well as interpret reliably in this thesis. The study elaborated on how sensory ethnography adds rich, contextual insights beyond what quantitative data alone can provide.

div.head: Data analysis
div.p: The data analysis will be built up in two main sections, qualitative analysis and quantitative analysis.

The quantitative analysis will explore the relations between room manipulations (smell and soft materiality) and psycho-physiological stress. From the literature we learned that the personal preference might mediate the effect the sensory experience has on the psychophysiological stress, therefore the quantitative parts of the sensory diary will be analysed here as well. Figure 6 shows a representation of a mediation analysis. The quantitative section will first analyse the separate paths. It will analyse relations between the room conditions (smell and softness) and psychological stress and physiological stress (path c), then similar analyses on the relation between the room conditions and the sensory appraisal (path a), and then a mixed analysis on the effects of sensory appraisals on psychological stress and physiological stress (path b). If all these analyses are significant, a mediation analysis will be performed. If one of these paths is not significant, there would be no indication of a mediation effect and would therefore not be performed. All statistical analyses are performed in Stata BE 18 (64Bit). The qualitative analysis will consist of a thematic analysis concerning the open questions of the sensory diaries and the focus groups. To remain as unbiased as possible, the different data types were first analysed separately before being compared.

div.head: Psychological stress
div.p: To analyse the effect room conditions have on psychological stress, a two-way repeated Anova's have been performed. These models have been tested for normality of the residuals using a Shapiro-Wilk test. The sphericity was not tested for as there is a degree of freedom = 1. When the normality assumption was not met, transformations were tried. If they did not improve the normality, a Mixed model would have been performed, as they are more robust.
The open-ended responses from the diary entries were thematically coded using the same coding scheme as the interviews, which will be elaborated on more in the next section of the focus groups.

div.head: Focus groups/ interviews
div.p: The data obtained from the focus groups was analysed using thematic analysis. First, the audio recordings were transcribed verbatim using transcribing software Alice and checked manually.

Subsequently, an initial set of codes was developed based on the research question and recurring patterns or terms from the data to capture participants' experiences. The transcripts were then systematically coded, allowing for the emergence of new codes when necessary. At the end, the transcripts were revisited to ensure that all relevant data was coded appropriately with the newly emerged codes included.

To gain overall insights, a matrix was created to examine the frequency and distribution of codes across the dataset setting out the codes per transcript. Additionally, relationships between codes were explored in a interaction matrix to identify patterns and connections. For the theme development step the codes were organised into meaningful groups, revealing patterns and relationships that provide insights into the research question. This process moves from detailed code analysis to a more abstract interpretation, where themes emerge. These themes are more than recurring elements-they represent deeper, patterned meanings that connect the research questions to the data.

div.head: Study Overview
div.p: This study aims to explore your sensory experience and psycho-physiological stress in a working environment. During the study:
• You will work in four different rooms, each designed to offer distinct experiences.
• We will measure your heart rate variability, skin conductance, and activity using a wearable sensor and sensors on two fingertips.
• At the end of each hour in a room, you will complete a short questionnaire about your mood and sensory experience.

• At the end of the day, there will be a focus group discussion with all participants to reflect on your experiences in greater depth. This starts at 16:15, the location will be made known at the start of the experiment.

div.head: Before the Study
div.p: To ensure accurate measurements:
• Avoid excessive alcohol the evening before the study.
• Refrain from caffeinated drinks (e.g., coffee, tea, energy drinks) for at least one hour before the study.

• Please wear a loose shirt, as we have to place electrode stickers on your collarbones and underneath your rib cage (please contact Annique if you do not feel comfortable with the placement of these electrodes).
• Download the m-Path app (See logo in the right), via which you can fill in the questionnaires.
• Arrive on time, at Atlas general purpose lab 1: room 9.126. Please use the toilet before the study, and try to refrain from having to get up during the study.

div.head: During the Study
div.p: To maintain the quality of the data:
• Perform your usual solitary tasks (no meetings or calls).
• Avoid highly stressful tasks. If unavoidable, inform the researcher, Annique.
• Do not adjust the sensors. If they feel uncomfortable or malfunction, please contact Annique.
• Do not eat or drink caffeinated items. Snacks can be enjoyed during wash-out periods. You can bring water or other non-caffeinated drinks.
• Wifi will be available in the rooms • Take your time to evaluate the room and fill out the questionnaire thoughtfully.
• During wash-out periods, you may walk around or stay in the reserved room. Do make sure to be on time at the next room.
